questions: Did s-bend line_loss_events fall below 1.0, and did s-bend progress rise above 0.68?
Did slalom line_loss_events return toward 1.0 from 1.85, with progress above 0.17?
Did steering_oscillation stay under about 0.35 on the oval and s-bend with the lighter, shorter body? If it rose, is the cause the faster yaw response or the lower mass?
Does the oval still finish 20 of 20 with max_error near 0.025?
If the s-bend stays at the 0.06 floor, is the limit now controller gain, so the next step is a controller change rather than geometry?

intent: Reduce yaw inertia (body_length 0.16 to 0.12 m, mass 0.8 to 0.6 kg) to give the robot a faster heading response on the s-bend and slalom, while reverting the sensor footprint to 0.012 m, which had the better overall score and oval reliability. Keep the sensor layout and wheel_track 0.09 fixed so the only change is inertia.
learning: Iteration 4 showed the 16 mm footprint restores slalom line retention (1.85 to 1.2 losses) but costs oval finishes (20 to 16 of 20) and lowers slalom progress, so the net score fell. The 12 mm footprint is kept. The s-bend remains the binding track, limited at the 0.06 m floor by turn authority. Yaw inertia is a geometry lever that the earlier iterations have not tried, and this iteration tests it.
rationale:
Iteration 4 (score 392, down from 449) tested sensor_size 0.016 on the iteration 3 design. It did not help overall. The slalom recovered from 1.85 to 1.2 line losses, which is close to the 1.0 target, but slalom progress fell to 0.12 and the oval dropped from 20 of 20 finishes to 16 of 20, with 4 off-track ends. The s-bend was unchanged at 1.05 line losses, with max_error at the 0.06 m floor and 2 of 20 finishes. Oscillation stayed under the 0.35 threshold on every track (oval 0.26, s-bend 0.29), so the blurred edge signal did not produce jitter. The larger footprint trades oval reliability for slalom line retention, and the net score fell. I therefore revert sensor_size to 0.012, which gives the best measured score (449 at iteration 3).

The s-bend is still limited at the 0.06 m floor with 1.0 line losses under both footprints. Narrowing wheel_track from 0.10 to 0.09 raised s-bend progress (0.64 to 0.68), so turn authority is still part of the limit. Narrowing further to 0.085 would likely worsen the slalom, which already lost 1.85 times per run at 0.09. I want a different lever that makes the robot turn more readily without narrowing the track. Yaw inertia is mass*(body_length^2 + body_width^2)/12. The current value is about 0.0027 kg·m². Shortening body_length from 0.16 to 0.12 m and reducing mass from 0.8 to 0.6 kg cuts it to about 0.0014 kg·m², roughly halved. A lower yaw inertia should let the wheel difference change heading faster, which helps the alternating bends of the s-bend and slalom. Body length has no effect on the off-track limit, which stays at 0.06 m. The lower mass also helps the 1.5 m/s pace needed to finish in 3 s.

The change is: body_length 0.16 to 0.12, mass 0.8 to 0.6, sensor_size back to 0.012, sensor y held at 0.07 and x unchanged, wheel_track 0.09, wheel_radius 0.03. Expected result: s-bend line_loss_events below 1.0, s-bend progress above 0.68, slalom line losses back toward 1.0, and the oval still finishing about 20 of 20. Risk: a lighter, shorter robot may oscillate more on the oval and may slip more under acceleration, so I will watch steering_oscillation (threshold about 0.35) and oval finish rate.
